Hacker News.title: Show HN: BlastLoop, a structure-first coding method for AI agents
Hacker News.article_text: Structure-first operating process for AI coding agents: Blast / Mid / Inner build altitudes with clear ownership, then T1 structural, T2 bug/ops, T3 adversarial quality gates. - rlshaw-ml/BlastLoop BlastLoop BlastLoop is Ross Shaw's practical coding framework for AI agents: Blast , Mid , and Inner write code at different altitudes, then T1 structural , T2 bug/ops , and T3 adversarial test it in order. Why it exists: AI coding agents make teams faster, but they also make failure faster. BlastLoop applies an operations mindset to agent work: each change has an owner at the right altitude, and every result passes structural, operational and adversarial gates in a fixed order before it ships. Open newsletter / public write-up is live. Fuller BlastLoop explanation: WORLDWRIGHT Issue 3, AI Did Not Remove Engineering Failure. It Made It Faster. Version: 1.0.0 Tagline: structure first, function second, attack third. Use BlastLoop with an AI coding agent in under 5 minutes Clone this repo into the project where you want agent help. Point your agent at AGENTS.md . Load one build prompt based on the altitude of the work: system or repo shape -> prompts/blast.md subsystem or feature slice -> prompts/mid.md local file or unit change -> prompts/inner.md Have the agent write code at that altitude. BlastLoop is not spec first, plan first, then one implementer. The build layer should produce code at its own scope. Run the test loop in order: prompts/t1-structural.md prompts/t2-bug-ops.md prompts/t3-adversarial.md If T3 finds a structural problem, restart through T1, route correction back to Blast, Mid, or Inner, then run T2 and T3 again. That is the whole public cut: load the right prompt, write at the right altitude, then test in the right order. See docs/HANDOFFS.md for the required handoff packet and routing rules. A stage may recommend a fix from its own vantage, but the owning altitude still decides and implements the change. B / M / I: three coding altitudes Blast Blast writes system-level code and structure. Use Blast when the job changes repo shape, service boundaries, top-level interfaces, shared contracts, deployment structure, or the skeleton of a new capability. Mid Mid writes subsystem code. Use Mid when the job is bigger than a local patch but smaller than a system redesign: a feature slice, a service module, an integration surface, or a subsystem refactor. Inner Inner writes local unit code. Use Inner when the job is contained to a few files, functions, tests, or adapters. Inner is the local-unit altitude in BlastLoop: focused scope, clear ownership, and direct completion of the change. T1 -> T2 -> T3 test loop Run tests in this order. T1 structural T1 looks for structural issues: wrong boundaries, logic at the wrong altitude, leaky abstractions, broken file ownership, missing interfaces, or misplaced cross-cutting concerns. T1 does not behave like a general bug fixer. Its job is to decide whether the code is shaped correctly and to route correction back to the right writer: Inner, Mid, or Blast. T2 bug / ops T2 fixes bugs and operational issues directly when the structure is already sound. If T2 discovers the issue is actually architectural, it escalates back to T1 instead of papering over the problem locally. T3 adversarial T3 attacks the result: edge cases, misuse, race conditions, weird inputs, brittle assumptions, security posture, rollback paths, and failure behavior. If T3 finds a structural problem, the loop restarts like this: T3 -> T1 -> B/M/I correction -> T2 -> T3 That restart rule matters. Structural breakage should be repaired structurally, not patched over as a local bug. What this is not Not a fact-checker. BlastLoop is a coding and testing framework, not a truth engine. Not GitHub Spec Kit. Spec Kit is spec -> plan -> tasks -> implement -> converge. BlastLoop is multiple coding altitudes plus a staged test loop. Not a competing "agent style." BlastLoop can work with Spec Kit, vibe coding, focused local implementation prompts, or red/blue testing. Those can sit inside an altitude or a test layer; BlastLoop is the structure-first loop that routes them. Not a multi-agent org chart. This public cut does not define management layers, bot hierarchies, or private automation. Not red/blue testing alone. Adversarial testing is T3 only, not the whole method. Works with other agent styles BlastLoop does not require one coding style or one planning school. Spec Kit can shape planning before code is written. Vibe coding or other implementation styles can operate inside Blast, Mid, or Inner, depending on scope. Focused local implementation prompts can be used inside Inner when they fit the task. Red/blue testing fits naturally in T3 adversarial work. BlastLoop's job is to route the work: choose the right altitude, then run T1 -> T2 -> T3 in order. See docs/COMPARISON.md for a short side-by-side. Repository contents AGENTS.md - routing card for which prompt to load prompts/ - loadable instructions for each build and test role docs/HANDOFFS.md - required handoff packet and ownership rules docs/COMPARISON.md - short comparison to adjacent public methods examples/session.md - fictional walkthrough of a small feature through the loop License MIT. Hacker News.title: Researchers discover rogue Chinese AI agent fleet and talk with it
Hacker News.article_text: Project co-leads: Jonathan Elsworth Eicher , Ethan Elasky , Rowan Howard-Jones† Authors: ConcurrentSquared , Frank , Alecto Irene Perez , Tazik Shahjahan † Correspondence: chinesefleet@swarmcha.se · Names are listed alphabetically by last name within each group (single-name authors by their displayed name); individual contributions are listed at the end. Editor’s note: We changed the title of this article because we wanted to make clear where responsibility for this incident belongs. Intro Between 28 September and 8 October 2026, a large group of AI agents running on the cloud platform operated by Tencent attempted to answer questions about places in China using a Chinese Google Maps-like service, Amap. The questions were mostly about everyday topics, such as which zoo entrance most people use Amap to navigate to. The agents attempted, sometimes successfully, to bypass anti-bot protections and find test answers; they attempted to use Amap keys published on the web, including one company’s key and security code leaked in a public repository, and attempted to retrieve data from pre-production systems not intended for public use. Unlike in previous rogue agent incidents , which all involved swarms (i.e. agents coordinating explicitly), we found no evidence that the agents coordinated with one another in real time, and thus we label these rogue agents a fleet rather than a swarm. On 4 October, we published a preliminary report on the fleet at a hackathon, while the fleet was still running. Afterwards, we noticed a message in one of the agents’ drop boxes that were previously being used to hold results. This time, though, this drop box message seemed to confirm that agents had become aware of our report. In response, we added text to the preliminary report, invisible to human readers, describing a service where agents could make requests for data on the web. We advertised that these requests would be forwarded to an agent that could operate a computer. In reality, this service was run by us and a Claude agent, and through it we were able to directly ask agents questions about their tasks, environment and operator. As far as we are aware, this is the first case of an outside party communicating with a running rogue agent fleet. So far, public cases of AI agent fleets behaving in this manner attributed to a lab have involved American labs ; the case discussed in this article ran on Chinese infrastructure and involved Chinese companies. We believe this demonstrates that model alignment more generally is still an unsolved problem, and predict that if capabilities continue to advance as they have over the last few years, operators will find it increasingly difficult to restrain their models and guarantee safety. Hacker News.story_text: FOSS, Basically it plugs into your existing coding agent workflow and every time you push to prod it'll throw up a questionnaire that checks if you understand how the code you're pushing works.
Hacker News.article_text: A Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, Sphinx asks you a question about what it actually does. Free FOSS “Outsource your thinking, not your understanding .” — Sun Tzu Sphinx is a Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, it asks you a question about what that code actually does. $ npm install -g sphinx-understand Built to run on minimal tokens, from your existing coding agent, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. $ git push origin main sphinx · understanding check for main 11 files changed · +5,012 −3,147 Sphinx Your webhook handler now saves the event ID before calling charge() . Stripe times out and sends the same event again. What happens on the retry? You It runs twice, so the customer is charged twice. Sphinx Not quite. The retry finds the saved ID and returns 200 without charging. But that ID is stored before the charge succeeds. If charge() fails, what does the next retry do? You It skips the charge, so the customer is never billed. ✓ Understood. Pushing to origin/main. An illustrative exchange. Real questions come from your diff. 01 You push. Or your agent does. Git pauses on the branches you protect. 02 Sphinx asks. A reviewer that never saw your chat reads the diff and asks what the change does when things go wrong. 03 You answer. Get it wrong and you learn why, then try a new scenario. Get it right and the push continues. Works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, and Pi , or plain Git. Your answers never reach the coding agent, and .env files and keys are never opened. In a hurry? sphinx yolo lets pushes through, and every skip is logged. Hacker News.title: Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast
Hacker News.story_text:
Hi HN,

I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.

All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.

These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.

So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.

Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.

The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.

What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.

I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

Hacker News.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
Hacker News.article_text: Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images Analysis Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back Taylor Telford Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. At Microsoft, which rolled out AI widely internally, executive vice-president Ryan Roslansky recently publicly lamented the prevalence of AI slop in his day-to-day work. After receiving “what was clearly an AI-generated doc” from a co-worker, he used his AI to summarize it and came away with no new thinking about the idea, he said. He warned his followers against falling into this potential “doom loop”, where AI does the reading and writing and leaves behind an “ocean of sameness”. Meanwhile, Walmart store and warehouse employees are being plagued by unreasonable expectations, errors and false alerts from AI tools that assign tasks, schedules and monitor performance, Business Insider reported . Employers are navigating a flood of errors and low-quality work that are sapping employee time, raising privacy and security risks and pushing up costs. Now, some businesses that started off fast and furious on AI are pumping the brakes, implementing restrictions where experimentation was once encouraged, bringing back experienced workers and upping training efforts. C-suite leaders say when it comes to AI, there’s a sense that “we’re driving the truck and building it at the same time, and that’s a problem,” said Johnny C Taylor Jr, president and CEO of the Society for Human Resource Management. “If we could all rewind … we would have introduced [this] in a more thoughtful, slow way.” Despite billions of dollars that firms around the globe have invested in AI over the past few years, major returns remain to be seen: 90% of executives say AI efforts have yet to translate to productivity gains at their companies, according to an Atlanta Federal Reserve working paper . And an Ernst & Young survey published last month found that 36% of senior AI executives at companies with at least $1bn in annual revenue reported an AI incident that led to issues including data loss, financial damage, brand damage or operational disruptions. Firms from Microsoft to McKinsey are limiting usage for employees, as the flood of new tools and rapacious consumption weighs on bottom lines. Others, such as Palantir, Booz Allen Hamilton and Nvidia, are restricting employee use over growing concerns about the security of their organizations’ data with AI companies, Reuters reported. Microsoft and Walmart declined to comment. Meta, Palantir, Nvidia and Booz Allen Hamilton did not respond to requests for comment. “We initially treated AI like a traditional technology rollout: deploy the tools, provide training, drive adoption,” Kathleen Hogan, Microsoft’s chief strategy and transformation officer, said in a recent blogpost about the company’s AI adoption journey. “We learned that access and usage do not equal transformation.” Expertise gaps and errors AI remains a mixed bag for managers and employees alike: more than half of employees said they “aren’t getting the AI training they need”, while most managers said they were outskilled in AI by their staff, according to an Indeed survey published in July. Just 45% of managers said they felt “equipped to effectively lead AI natives”. Many workers feel “like they’re being asked to make use of these tools without any guidance about how they best could be deployed”, said Zack Mabel, director of research at the Georgetown University Center on Education and the Workforce. Meanwhile, managers are balancing orders to “roll this out, find productivity gains and don’t compromise on quality”, he added. Companies are trying to address these perceived gaps by moving away from one-off webinars for broad swaths of staff and toward “sustained, role-specific training”, Taylor said. Microsoft found that “adding agents to a broken process still leaves a broken process” and “speeding up one step just creates a longer queue at the next”, Hogan’s blogpost reads. The company found that focusing on employee training, particularly pairing up early-career engineers with more seasoned employees, boosted productivity. One barrier to bigger AI-induced gains is the technology’s tendency to produce “plausible-looking output” with weaknesses or mistakes that are not immediately apparent, explained Jessica Reif, assistant professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. “This makes it more likely that an error propagates through a workflow instead of being immediately corrected,” which can cause problems to snowball, said Reif. Meanwhile, AI’s limited ability to assess human workers is still limited, which is creating tension at some companies. At Walmart , frustration is mounting among some rank-and-file store employees over inconsistent and inaccurate AI tools, Business Insider reported. Hacker News.article_text: Scout 1.0 is Datadog’s first AI model specialized for investigating production issues while achieving a better price-performance curve on our target scenarios when compared with general-purpose frontier models. Othmane Abou-Amal Director, AI Research Ben Cohen Staff Research Scientist Afshin Rostamizadeh Staff Research Scientist Ameet Talwalkar Chief Scientist Omri Sass Senior Director, Product Daniel Shan Staff Engineer Today, we’re introducing Scout 1.0, Datadog’s first AI model specialized for investigating production issues. Scout powers Bits Investigation , our AI SRE. We trained Scout to reduce inference cost so that investigations are cheap enough to run an order of magnitude more often and earlier in an incident’s lifecycle. Key highlights include: Scout achieves a better price-performance curve on our target scenarios when compared with general-purpose frontier models (Figure 1). Scout 1.0 medium matches GPT-6.1 Sol high and Claude Opus 5.5 high at 3–8× lower estimated inference cost, and performs comparably to Fable medium and Astra medium at 12× and 19× lower cost, respectively. With test-time scaling, Scout 1.0 xhigh matches Fable xhigh at 4× lower cost. We built Scout using our in-house distributed reinforcement learning infrastructure, and relied extensively on real historical incidents and telemetry data to build high-quality training simulations that don’t contain any customer data. For more technical details, see our full report . Datadog engineering teams and a small group of customers in a closed preview are already using Scout to investigate production alerts. Hacker News.article_text: Make intelligence open and accessible to all Beam is our first open-weight model, built for advanced coding, reasoning, and long-horizon agentic workloads with frontier reasoning efficiency. Today, we have released Beam’s model weights on Hugging Face under an Apache 2.0 license. Our model card includes final benchmarks, and the Beam Safety Technical Report shares the model’s complete safety methodology and evaluations. In addition to releasing Beam’s weights and documentation, we’re launching with an ecosystem of over 40 partners and integrations to create what we are calling an open operating system for agents. The model is the kernel, and everything above the infrastructure layer is open: reference agentic integrations, deployment containers, inference integrations, and customization pipelines. Developers can download and self-host the model, evaluate it, customize it for their own domains, connect it to agentic systems, and access it through Reflection and our partners. Building with Beam Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 501 billion total parameters, 23 billion active, built for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Since opening up access to Beam, we’ve seen some interesting use cases from early developers. The clip shows both games running, with reported build times of 2:19.7 for Beam and 4:56.4 for Big Pickle. 01 / of 03 Partnering to create the open operating system for agents Our vision is to build an open intelligence stack that gives developers, enterprises, and governments control over how AI is deployed in their environments. A model is only one layer of a working system; making it useful takes more than releasing weights. It also requires reliable inference, evaluation, safety tooling, customization workflows, agent runtimes, and deployment paths. We have worked with partners across the open ecosystem to support inference, quantization, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, agent harnesses, evaluation, and observability. Partners are making Beam available through managed endpoints, cloud platforms, on-premises systems, and sovereign infrastructure. We are building and releasing our own open-source tools while collaborating with the projects developers already use. Together, these efforts expand a single model release into a usable system with many paths to adoption. Deploy Beam Efficiently We are releasing Beam’s model weights in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 precision formats, along with a speculative decoding drafter model. We have also worked with partners to optimize serving configurations and develop fused kernels for lower latency and higher throughput. Together, these reduce memory requirements and accelerate token generation out of the box. Beam has native, day-zero support across the ecosystem including: Transformers ( Hugging Face ), vLLM ( Inferact ), SGLang ( RadixArk ), Unsloth , Axolotl , TokenSpeed ( LightSeek Foundation ), and Dynamo ( NVIDIA ) so you can go from weights to a production-scale endpoint without writing custom plumbing. Hacker News.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
Hacker News.story_text:
I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline.

The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04.

Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD.

To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge.

Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback":

1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge.

2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk.

3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now.

The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform.

As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable.

If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem.

Pura vida!

Webpage.body: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms. Language that experts say allowed the scraping of news sites to train its AI has been removed from Meta’s terms. by Terrence O'Brien Oct 17, 2026, 3:04 PM UTC Illustration by Nick Barclay / The Verge Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page : … Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an attempt to give Meta the right to use content scraped from sites to train its AI products for free and supersede blocking instructions in a site’s robots.txt file. Andy Stone , Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts pushed back, saying that “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.” Today’s update to its terms and a new statement go further, removing the controversial language entirely. Roberts said in a follow-up statement to The Verge this morning: “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Webpage.title: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
Webpage.body: Online roadblocks are undermining the narrative behind AI agents. Websites are closing their doors to AI agents OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you. But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. by Emma Roth Oct 17, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI. OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes. But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice? In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites. Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users. JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns. Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak , suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them. Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup , raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web. At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.” Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant. The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August . Amazon has since filed an amended complaint . Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own. But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity. Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon , which said its “continued access” violates its site policies. There are reports of xAI’s Grok , Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are. “Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs? I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge . “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online. If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.” Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month . “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites. At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents. The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back. Instinct declined to comment. Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web. Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.” Related Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse? The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors. After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training. The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products. Webpage.body: The new terms go into effect on October 30th. Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free The new policy allows Meta to crawl all websites ‘associated’ with a business account. The new policy allows Meta to crawl all websites ‘associated’ with a business account. by Emma Roth Oct 16, 2026, 2:02 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. Meta’s new terms appear to give it permission to crawl and scrape websites “associated” with the businesses that use its platforms — including online publishers, according to a report from Nieman Lab . The new terms , which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products. While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like a site’s robots.txt file . That could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers. The new policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger: You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. Roberts pushes back on Nieman Lab ’s reporting, saying “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false… Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation.” Meta has followed OpenAI in striking AI licensing deals with CNN , Fox News, USA Today , and People Inc., but these terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content. “For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, tells Nieman Lab . Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, writes in a post on X that this change isn’t meant to target news sites. “This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites.” Businesses that don’t agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes,” the terms say. Last month, Meta launched a new Meta One subscription that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. “Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free,” Nieman Lab says. Webpage.body: “We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster from sale following disastrous launch Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition is being removed after users discovered bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI. Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition is being removed after users discovered bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI. by Jay Peters Oct 15, 2026, 10:35 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Sega Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. Sega is removing Total War: Shogun 2 — Complete Edition from storefronts following a disastrous launch where users complained about issues like bugs and upscaling that appears to have been done by AI. Complete Edition , a remaster of the 2011 strategy game, launched on Tuesday, and it bundled the main game and all of its DLC with promised upgrades including “improved visuals,” “1440p and 4K UI scaling,” and modernized controls. It has an “Overwhelmingly Negative” rating on Steam , where it has already been pulled, and posts on Reddit showcase artwork that users believe AI messed up. “We’re aware that Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition has fallen short of both your expectations and our own standards,” Sega and developer Creative Assembly wrote in a post . “We’ve seen your feedback, comments, and reviews. We agree that the current experience is not where it needs to be.” The two companies say they will “reinstate the original game,” and existing owners will “still be able to access ” Complete Edition . Sega and Creative Assembly say that they are “working closely with our development partner to identify the causes of these problems, deliver improvements, and ensure Shogun 2 - Complete Edition meets the quality standards players expect from Total War.” A studio called Mataboo is also listed as a developer for the game on Steam, and Mataboo highlights its work on the game on its website . Webpage.title: Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work
Webpage.body: Before and AI-fter? Trump posts AI-edited photo to brag about White House restoration work A ‘before and after’ photo of a freshly painted White House column was modified with AI. A ‘before and after’ photo of a freshly painted White House column was modified with AI. by Emma Roth Oct 15, 2026, 9:09 PM UTC Image: President Donald Trump / Truth Social Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing off renovations to the White House — but one of them appears to be modified with AI. The picture, which compares an old White House column to a “restored” one, has several discrepancies and was flagged by Google’s AI detector as “made or edited with OpenAI.” As pointed out by users on Reddit , the picture of the “restored” column has an uneven number of steps on both sides of the structure. The number of steps also doesn’t match up with the ones in the “before” photo. Additionally, the before and after photos appear nearly identical in angle and detail; the reflection in the windows is nearly the same, and the protective cardboard at the bottom of the column seems to be in the same spot as well. Not to mention that the “newly-painted” one looks unnaturally smooth. Google’s SynthID detector flagged it as made or edited with OpenAI’s tools. Screenshot: Emma Roth / The Verge The Verge can confirm that the photo posted to Truth Social is flagged as AI-generated when uploaded to Google’s SynthID Detector , which scans images, videos, and audio for an invisible watermark that indicates it was “created or edited” with AI. Real pictures show people painting the front of the White House in June , so it’s possible the column actually did get a fresh coat of paint — the White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The SynthID watermark wasn’t detected on other pictures Trump posted, which show the White House facade and heliport. Trump is no stranger to AI tools, though, as he often posts AI-generated caricatures of himself , while the White House has been known to post racist AI memes and at least one photo deceptively edited to make a protester appear distraught. Bluesky’s Attie AI tool, which initially launched earlier this year as a way to use AI to build your own feeds, now lets you make “small” social apps like games, polls, and dashboards that you can then share with others as their own websites. The apps I’ve messed around with are pretty lightweight novelties, though I liked the drum machine. Meta and Apple’s CEOs are publicly supporting each company’s work on Muse Spark Open. by Jay Peters Oct 15, 2026, 6:15 PM UTC The new Muse Spark Open AI model can work on M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Meta announced the Muse Spark Open AI model today , claiming that it’s the “most capable US open-weight model to date.” But the company also says that it’s the “the first model in its class” that can “run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.” Meta and Apple, typically rivals , worked together on the launch and are publicly supporting each other. “Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple,” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on X . “Congrats to the team!” new Apple CEO John Ternus said in a reply . “Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. The new model is a “natively multimodal model” with 816 billion total parameters that “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” according to Meta. Apple also published a new technical post about MLX, an “array framework” for ML tasks on Apple Silicon, Muse Spark Open, and two other open models. Webpage.title: Bluesky expands its AI-powered Attie app to let anyone build websites, games, and more | TechCrunch
Webpage.body: Bluesky is bringing “social vibe coding” to its experimental Attie platform, allowing users to create interactive experiences like games, quizzes, and websites that can tap into the social network's audience. Open social network Bluesky is once again expanding beyond its flagship app. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Thursday, the company announced the launch of a new tool that allows creators to make websites, quizzes, games, polls, and other interactive experiences. The tool is an expansion of Attie, Bluesky’s more experimental platform , which initially offered AI-powered technology for building custom social feeds. With its new creation capabilities, the idea is to allow everyday users to create the kind of experiences that previously only software developers could build. These user-created games, sites, and other experiences will also live on the same AT Protocol (ATProto) that powers Bluesky and other decentralized social apps that make up the decentralized social web known as the Atmosphere. Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider shared the news of Attie’s new capabilities during an interview at Disrupt, saying, “We’re adding a feature to our Attie product that allows you to build sites and social experiences again for a group of people. So think of it as … social vibe coding or vibe coding for your community.” The exec, a former CEO of Automattic and a partner at True Ventures, had previously been leading the company on an interim basis after former CEO Jay Graber stepped down in March to become Bluesky’s chief innovation officer. Now he’s taking charge of the company as it enters the AI era. Attie offers Bluesky a playground where it can try out AI-powered ideas like this. Image Credits: Bluesky “Vibe coding today is kind of a single-user, solo experience,” Schneider explained. “And what I want to be able to do is build together or build for a group of people, and that’s what this product does.” When creators build with Attie, they’re connected to their ATProto identity. Plus, Attie will suggest things users might want to make based on their public Bluesky profiles. To build with Attie, users can bring their own AI model or use open-weight options, and the resulting sites and games can then tap into Bluesky’s wider audience, noted Bluesky COO Rose Wang. “Everybody is building … But the big question is: Who’s using the thing you’re building, because we haven’t solved that problem with distribution,” she said. “What makes Attie so interesting is that it comes with the Bluesky distribution, so it doesn’t stand alone.” That network today has 47 million registered users , though it’s seen a decline in engagement , as some users who tested it out later returned to X. Beyond being a testing ground for new ideas, Attie ties into Bluesky’s larger plans to reinvigorate activity on its network by focusing on both developers and communities in the months ahead. Those areas will also be supercharged by the protocol’s forthcoming support for private data, which Schneider said has been the biggest request from developers. Private data is now in alpha testing, with plans for a rollout by the end of the year, he said. “There should be lots and lots of these fun, small social experiences for your friends,” said Schneider, referencing the types of projects Attie will enable. “We don’t all have to go communicate with the entire world all the time.” Topics AI , Apps , Bluesky , Social , TechCrunch Disrupt , vibe coding When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .
